title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.
lineage: mutation of I0428 ('Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte's Demand Package Review is carrier-side workflow (nurse review, 3-10 days, no LOP framing, no signature, no testimony). This is counsel-facing work product, signed and testifiable, and Enlyte reviewers can refer files to us for the signature layer instead of us fighting them for carriers. FAIR Health is a data input and the plaintiff expert's favorite anchor, so the kit pre-rebuts it instead of selling benchmarks. EvenUp is plaintiff-only and its demand packages become our intake format. Turquoise and CLARA sell rate analytics or claims software, not signed opinions. JurisPro-style billing experts are bespoke at $3-5k and slow. We take the repeatable 80% at a tenth of the price and hand the firm an expert only when a file justifies it. Starting in Georgia and Texas avoids Florida's statutory benchmark, and using payer and Medicare anchors avoids the weak hospital-file why-now.

competitors.name: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions
competitors.what_they_do: Incumbent carrier vendor. Turns plaintiff demand packages into structured reports: bill data capture, duplicate detection, coding and summaries, and a nurse-review tier for causation and treatment. Benchmarks 'costs, severity, and treatment duration against industry data'. Advertises a '60% average reduction in medical charges' and '$5-7K improvement in average settlement'. Turnaround is 3-4 days for the enhanced review and about 10 days for the nurse review. The page does not mention LOP, a certified-coder signature, expert declarations or testimony. Enlyte could add those, and it already owns the carrier relationships and workflow.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large established vendor (Enlyte). No funding figure found. Adjacent to the idea's carrier segment, and the biggest incumbent risk.

competitors.name: FAIR Health
competitors.what_they_do: Nonprofit that sells charge and allowed-amount benchmark data. Its site lists 'Liability' and 'Legal' (law firms, bill review services) as industries served, and describes FAIR Health as an official data source for PIP, workers' comp and surprise-billing programs. It is more likely a data input for this idea than a competitor. Its benchmarks are also the standard 'usual and customary' reference a plaintiff expert would cite against the report.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established nonprofit data utility. No litigation-report product confirmed on the pages I could fetch.

competitors.name: EvenUp
competitors.what_they_do: Plaintiff-side personal injury AI platform covering intake, treatment tracking ('Medical Management'), demands, negotiation, discovery and trial. Plaintiff-only, with no defense products or bill-analysis product visible. It matters because it arms the other side of every LOP case. Its demand packages and treatment tracking make the bills you would rebut more polished and better documented.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Series E of $150M at a $2B+ valuation (Oct 2025), per its newsroom at https://www.evenuplaw.com/newsroom. Announced a LexisNexis alliance in Sept 2026.

competitors.name: Turquoise Health
competitors.what_they_do: Price-transparency platform (Analyze, Contracts, Compliance) selling rate analytics to providers, payers, employers and life-sciences firms. Its pages make no mention of litigation or personal injury. It is a plausible data supplier or a possible future entrant. It is not a current competitor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Says it has '300+' healthcare organizations as partners. No funding figure found.

competitors.name: CLARA Analytics
competitors.what_they_do: AI claims analytics for workers' comp, auto liability and general liability (Document Intelligence, Triage, Treatment, Litigation, Fraud). Its pages don't mention BI medical bill benchmarking, LOP or reasonable value. It sells software to carriers rather than coder-signed evidence.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed insurtech. I did not verify the funding amount.

competitors.name: Independent billing/coding expert witnesses and expert-referral directories (for example JurisPro)
competitors.what_they_do: This is the substitute the idea targets, and the idea's own premise is that defense firms pay $3-5k per case for these experts. The JurisPro fetch confirmed only that the directory has a medical expert category. It showed no individual billing-expert profiles or fee ranges. Because the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200), I could not enumerate or verify the individual expert practices or any productized flat-fee competitor. That is the biggest hole in this check.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Fragmented cottage industry. No aggregate size found.

I0428.evidence_of_demand:
Partial evidence, all inferred from statute and vendor marketing. I found no forum complaints, RFPs or quoted willingness-to-pay for this exact product.

(1) Statute forcing the analysis. Florida 768.0427 requires claimants to disclose the LOP, itemized billing with procedure codes, any factoring company and the dollar amount it paid for the account, coverage status and who referred the treatment, and makes the law-firm/provider relationship admissible. That creates a structured record defense counsel has to analyze. Source: https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html and the bill page https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2023/837. I could not fetch the Georgia 2025 tort-reform text (legiscan returned 403), so the Georgia and other-state claims in the idea are unverified.

(2) Carriers already pay for adjacent outsourced bill analysis. Enlyte sells Demand Package Review as a paid service, with a nurse tier and a stated '60% average reduction in medical charges' and '$5-7K improvement in average settlement' (https://www.enlyte.com/solutions/casualty/cost-containment-services/demand-package-review). Enlyte also publishes content about 'Questionable Billing Patterns' in demands (https://www.enlyte.com/insights/article/injury-liability/bodily-injury-demand-review). These figures are vendor marketing.

(3) The plaintiff-side spending arms race. EvenUp raised $150M at a $2B+ valuation (Oct 2025) to build better demands and treatment management for plaintiff firms (https://www.evenuplaw.com/newsroom). It implies defense spend is likely to follow, but it is not direct proof.

(4) The idea's own premise, that experts cost $3-5k, is unverified. None found: forum threads, RFPs, or published prices for coder-signed reports.
I0428.sharper_angle: Narrow it and sell it as an evidence product, not a report. (1) Start in a state without a statutory Medicare-multiple benchmark, such as Georgia, Texas or Louisiana, where reasonable value is contested and a signed local benchmark carries more weight. Treat Florida as a rebuttal-of-plaintiff-expert product, since 768.0427 already supplies a free benchmark. (2) Build the report around the LOP disclosure record. Ingest the letter, the itemized coded bill, the factoring purchase price and the referral relationship. Compute the statutory or market benchmark, flag litigation-built billing patterns, and hand counsel cross-examination questions keyed to specific lines. The factoring price and referral facts are what a generic bill-review vendor won't tie together. (3) Make the testimony the profit center. Give reports away cheaply as lead generation, and sell the declaration and testimony ($1,500-3,500) as the margin. Build a library of transcripts and Daubert outcomes as the moat. (4) Sell first to volume defense firms and panel-counsel programs, which have the acute pain and are underserved by Enlyte-style carrier workflow tools. Approach carrier vendors like Enlyte as a partner that supplies the coder signature and testimony layer, rather than competing head-on. (5) Before committing, do the searches I could not run and check whether an established expert practice already sells flat-fee LOP reasonable-value reports in Florida or Georgia.
